Code tour storyboard

How the CrowdPulse code works

A 4:43 tour for someone who wants to understand the code: how it is laid out, and what runs on the app's main paths. The code is on the left, in a VS Code style editor showing the real source files; the app runs on the right. A line turns yellow when the app actually makes that call or receives that broadcast. Every image is a real frame of the render (from the 1440p master, shown at 1280×720), and the narration is the script the Kokoro af_heart voice reads. Scenes come from film/tour/tour.js.

0:00This is CrowdPulse, from the inside. On the right, the app, running. On the left, the code that’s running it.

0:09This isn’t a line by line walkthrough. It’s a map: how the code is laid out, and what runs when the app does its main jobs.

0:18How the code is laid out

Code
The Explorer, event.html’s script tags, then the SQL migration
App
A map of the code builds up: six pages, two helpers, and Supabase
Sound
Whoosh on the chapter card

0:18Start with the layout. Everything the browser loads is in the public folder: six plain HTML pages, with one script for each. No framework, and the build just copies files.

0:30Every page loads the same two helpers before its own script. common.js draws the shared pieces, like the gauge and the chart. supa.js is the connection to the back end.

0:44The back end is Supabase, and almost all of it is one SQL file: the tables, the security rules, and a function for every action. There’s no server of our own to run.

0:56One connection, two directions

Code
supa.js: CP.connect, emit and the Realtime listener
App
The map: calls go up through database functions, broadcasts come back down
Sound
Soft ticks as lines light up

0:56One idea holds it all together, and it lives in supa.js. Every page asks for a connection, and gets back a small socket with two methods.

1:07Emit sends something up. Each name maps to a database function: join, an admin action, or anything else an attendee does.

1:16And on listens for what comes back down: a Realtime broadcast, on a private channel that belongs to this one session.

1:24Up through a function, down through a broadcast. Every feature in the app is a variation on that loop.

1:31Joining a session

Code
home.js, then event.js beside the cp_join function
App
An attendee types the join code, picks a profile and lands in the lobby
Sound
Key taps, clicks

1:32Watch it happen. An attendee types a join code on the home page. home.js asks the database whether that session exists, then opens the attendee page.

1:43There, event.js connects and emits join. In the database, cp_join records the participant, and hands back a snapshot: everything the page needs to draw itself.

1:56From then on, the page keeps that snapshot as its state, and render functions turn state into screen. The session hasn’t started, so it draws the lobby.

2:06Going live

Code
control.js, the cp_admin function, then event.js’s event listener
App
The host presses Go live in the control room; the phone flips to rating
Sound
Click, pop

2:06Now the host. In the control room, the Go live button emits admin start.

2:13In the database, cp_admin checks that the caller really is an admin of this session, flips the status to live, and broadcasts the new event to everyone.

2:24On the phone, the event listener sees the status change and renders again. The lobby becomes the rating screen. Nobody refreshed anything.

2:33The live pulse

Code
event.js’s sendRating, cp_act and cp_do_rate, then cp_tick and the pulse listeners
App
A slider drag on the phone; the big screen’s gauge follows every two seconds
Sound
Soft ticks on every call and broadcast

2:33Here’s the heart of it. Dragging the slider calls send rating, which waits a quarter of a second, then emits rate.

2:42cp_act routes it to cp_do_rate, which stores the number against that participant. Notice what it doesn’t do: it doesn’t tell anyone.

2:52That’s the job of cp_tick. Every two seconds, the control room and the big screen call it. It averages the latest ratings, measures the energy, and broadcasts one small message: the pulse.

3:06Every screen is listening for it. On pulse updates the gauge, the bars and the chart, all drawn by the shared helpers in common.js.

3:17So a hundred people dragging sliders still means just one broadcast every two seconds.

3:23Everything else, same route

Code
event.js emits and listeners beside cp_act’s branches, then the grants at the end of the SQL file
App
Reactions and a chat message from the phone show up on the big screen
Sound
Taps, key taps

3:24Chat, questions, polls and reactions all take the same route. One line to emit, one branch in cp_act, and one listener to draw the result.

3:36And the rules live in the database, not the browser. The tables are closed. A browser can only call the functions granted at the bottom of the file, and each one checks who is calling.

3:49The report

Code
report.js and supa.js, then the report Edge Function and analytics.js
App
The report page loads and scrolls: grade, timeline, key moments
Sound
Chime as the report appears

3:49When the session ends, there’s one more path. report.js asks an Edge Function for the report.

3:57The function checks that you’re allowed to see it, reads the raw data with a key the browser never gets, and runs it through analytics.js, which turns ratings and chat into a grade, key moments and insights.

4:13Only crowd-level results come back, and Chart.js draws them.

4:18Outro

Code
The Explorer, with each part of the map lit in turn
App
The finished map, then the end card
Sound
Music resolves

4:19So that’s the map. Six pages, with a script each. One connection file. One SQL file that holds the rules. And one function for the report.

4:30To explore it yourself, run npm run dev, open a session’s control room, and start the built-in audience simulator. Then follow one emit, and see where it lands.
